issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette:
Vinh's Story

Vinh was twenty-three when the bombing happened. He had been working at the regional bank downtown for just over a year, a position that had made his parents proud-steady work, a uniform, a future that looked like stability. On a Tuesday morning in March, he was at his teller station when the blast came. He didn't hear it so much as feel it: a percussion that seemed to come from inside his own chest, followed by a chaos of sound and movement he could never quite reconstruct in order. People screaming. Glass everywhere. A woman's purse on the floor, its contents scattered. He remembered thinking, with a strange clarity, that he needed to help, that this was what a capable person would do. But his body wouldn't move. He stood frozen behind the counter while others rushed toward the exits, and it was only when a security guard grabbed his arm that he began to run.

Three people died in the bombing. Vinh survived without physical injury-not a scratch, which somehow felt like its own kind of damage. In the weeks that followed, he replayed that moment of paralysis obsessively, tormented by the conviction that he had failed in the most fundamental way. He had always understood himself as someone reliable, someone who could be counted on. His ex-wife, Sophia, had initially tried to be supportive, but his withdrawal from her was swift and complete. He couldn't bear to be close to anyone, couldn't tolerate the vulnerability of being truly known. The intimacy that had once felt natural now felt impossible-how could he let her see him as he now saw himself, as someone who had frozen while others needed help? By the time they separated fourteen months later, he had already begun the patterns that would come to define his days.

The overworking started almost immediately after the bombing. Vinh began arriving at the bank before opening and staying well past closing, volunteering for extra shifts, taking on tasks that belonged to other tellers. His supervisor noticed but said nothing; Vinh was reliable, efficient, never complained. What he was actually doing, though he wouldn't have articulated it this way, was making sure he was never alone with himself. The moment he stopped moving, the thoughts would come-the image of that purse on the floor, the sound of someone crying in the darkness, his own immobility. So he worked. He filled his mind with transaction codes and customer names and the mechanical rhythm of counting bills. At home, he did the same thing differently: he reorganized his apartment obsessively, fixed things that weren't broken, spent hours at the gym until his muscles burned. Anything to keep the thoughts at bay.

But the harder he worked to suppress what had happened, the more it seemed to seep into everything. His conviction that he was no longer capable of the things that had once defined him-reliability, courage, the ability to act in a crisis-deepened with each passing week. This wasn't a thought he could simply dismiss. It felt like a fact about who he had become. And this certainty about his own fundamental inadequacy began to feed something else: a constant, grinding sense of threat. He started waking in the night, his heart hammering, and would lie in bed checking the locks on his apartment door, sometimes getting up to verify them again. At the bank, he found himself frequently glancing over his shoulder, watching the faces of customers with a hypervigilance he couldn't control. Someone standing too close. A raised voice. The sight of a delivery truck pulling up to the curb. Each of these things triggered a spike of alarm that felt entirely reasonable to him-how could he trust the world not to betray him again, when he couldn't even trust himself to respond appropriately if it did?

The two years since the bombing had worn grooves into his life. His divorce had been finalized six months ago. His few friendships had atrophied as he declined invitations and failed to reach out. His work performance, despite the long hours, had begun to suffer; he made small errors, lost concentration mid-transaction, once snapped at a customer over a minor issue in a way that shocked them both. He had come to believe that he couldn't rely on himself-not to keep himself safe, not to be present for others, not to be the person he had once been. The checking and the waking and the constant vigilance were, in his mind, the only rational responses to a world that had proven itself dangerous and a self that had proven itself unequal to its demands. It was only when his mother, visiting from out of state, found him at three in the morning checking the windows for the fourth time that night, that she insisted he call someone. At twenty-six, Vinh finally made an appointment with a therapist, carrying with him the weight of four years of isolation and the conviction that seeking help was just another way of admitting how thoroughly he had failed.
